title: MANY WILL SAY, “LORD, LORD”… BUT JESUS WILL SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: MANY WILL SAY, “LORD, LORD”… BUT JESUS WILL SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”

The Most Terrifying Words in the Sermon on the Mount—And the Heartbreaking Truth About Religious People Who Look Saved, Sound Saved, and Even Do Things in Jesus’ Name, Yet Miss the One Person Who Can Save Them.
Imagine spending your entire life believing you were on your way to heaven…
Only to discover, when you finally stand before Jesus Christ, that you never truly belonged to Him.
Not because you had never heard His name.
Not because you had never opened a Bible.
Not because you were an atheist, an unbeliever, or someone who openly mocked God.
But because you had learned how to live around Jesus without ever surrendering your life to Jesus.
You knew the songs.
You knew when to say “Amen.”
You knew how to raise your hands during worship, how to quote Scripture when someone needed encouragement, how to speak about faith when life was going well.
Perhaps you even served in ministry.
Perhaps people looked up to you.
Perhaps someone once told you, “You are such a strong Christian.”
And you believed them.
But there was something happening beneath the surface that nobody could see.
A private compromise.
A cherished sin.
A heart growing comfortable with disobedience.
A religious identity that had slowly become a substitute for genuine fellowship with God.
And then comes the day when appearances no longer matter.
The crowd is gone.
The applause is silent.
The religious titles have lost their meaning.
There is only you…
And Jesus.
Then you hear the words you never imagined could be spoken to someone like you.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Matthew 7:23, KJV.
Read that again.
Not “I knew you once, but I forgot you.”
Not “You were too weak for Me.”
Not “You struggled too much.”
“I never knew you.”
Those words should disturb every person who has ever mistaken being familiar with Christianity for actually belonging to Christ.
But before fear drives you into despair, you need to understand something.
Jesus did not speak these words to destroy the hope of every struggling believer.
He spoke them to expose a deadly deception.
And buried inside this frightening warning is a truth so beautiful that it can change the way you understand salvation, repentance, obedience, and the grace of God.
Because the question is not simply whether you know enough about Jesus.
The question is whether you have truly come to Him.
And there is a difference.
A difference that eternity makes impossible to ignore.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus declares:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Matthew 7:21–23, KJV.
Notice something that makes this passage especially unsettling.
Jesus does not say a few will be surprised.
He says many.
And these people are not presented as strangers to religious activity.
They call Him “Lord.”
Twice.
They appeal to prophecy, deliverance, and mighty works performed in His name.
Their defense is not that they rejected Christianity.
Their defense is that they were deeply involved in things associated with Christianity.
Yet Jesus rejects their claim.
Why?
To understand that, we must listen carefully to what He actually said—not merely what generations of frightened Christians have assumed He meant.
In the original Greek of Matthew 7:21, the words translated “Lord, Lord” are:
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, kyrie.
Kyrie is the form of kyrios used when addressing someone as “Lord” or “Master.”
The repeated address communicates an urgent, emphatic appeal.
These people are not approaching Jesus casually.
They recognize Him as the One before whom they must answer.
But acknowledging His authority with their lips does not establish that they have lived under His authority.
That is the first uncomfortable truth.
A person can speak the language of surrender while continuing to live in rebellion.
You can call Jesus Lord on Sunday and spend the rest of the week acting as though He has no authority over your choices.
You can worship publicly while secretly protecting the very things His Word calls you to abandon.
You can defend biblical truth in arguments while refusing to let that same truth confront your own pride.
You can become skilled at recognizing sin in other people while remaining remarkably patient with your own.
And perhaps the most dangerous part?
You can become so accustomed to this divided life that eventually it stops bothering you.
What once convicted you becomes normal.
What once drove you to prayer becomes something you explain away.
What once made you weep before God becomes something you hide behind a smile.
And little by little, you learn to look spiritually alive while your heart drifts further from the One who gives life.
But Jesus sees what the crowd cannot.
He sees the private conversations.
The unspoken motives.
The bitterness you have dressed up as discernment.
The unforgiveness you have justified because somebody really did hurt you.
The secret compromises you keep promising to abandon tomorrow.
He also sees the wounds you never asked for, the battles you are exhausted from fighting, and the tears you have shed while begging Him to help you change.
That distinction matters.
Because there is a difference between someone who struggles against sin and someone who makes peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to repent.
There is a difference between being wounded and deliberately cultivating wickedness.
And Jesus knows the difference perfectly.
When He says, “I never knew you,” the original Greek reads:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς — oudepote egnōn hymas.
Literally, “I never knew you.”
The verb egnōn comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
In Scripture, knowing someone can mean more than possessing information about them. Depending on the context, it can describe personal recognition and relationship.
Jesus is not confessing ignorance.
He is not saying that He lacked information about these people.
The One who knows what is in humanity, as John 2:24–25 teaches, is not suddenly discovering unfamiliar faces.
His declaration is a rejection of their claim to belong to Him.
They may have claimed His name.
But He does not acknowledge them as His own.
And here is what should make us examine our hearts:
Their confidence was built on what they had done in His name—not on the saving mercy of the Christ they claimed to serve.
Listen to their defense.
“Have we not prophesied?”
“Have we not cast out devils?”
“Have we not done many wonderful works?”
Again and again, the emphasis falls on their accomplishments.
Their spiritual résumé.
Their visible achievements.
Their impressive religious history.
They are standing before the Savior, and their defense is a list of their works.
But no amount of religious achievement can substitute for reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Salvation is not a trophy awarded to the most religious person in the room.
It is a gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not church attendance.
Not a ministry title.
Not an impressive testimony.
Not the number of people who admire your spirituality.
Not even extraordinary works performed under a religious banner.
And certainly not the amount of money you have given.
Christ alone saves.
But then someone asks the question that makes this passage difficult.
“If salvation is by grace through faith, why does Jesus say that the one who enters the kingdom is the one who does the will of His Father?”
That question deserves a biblical answer, not a comforting slogan.
Because Jesus never taught that grace gives us permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
He also never taught that imperfect human obedience purchases eternal life.
The same passage in Ephesians that declares salvation to be a gift continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.”
Ephesians 2:10, KJV.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Obedience does not purchase salvation.
Genuine saving faith produces a changed direction of life.
Not sinless perfection.
Not a flawless spiritual record.
But repentance, growing trust, and a heart increasingly willing to submit to Jesus.
The grace that forgives us is also the grace that begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs believers to reject ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy bringing sinners into a new life.
And this is where Matthew 7 becomes deeply personal.
Because many of us have spent years asking God to bless the life we have built without ever seriously asking whether that life belongs to Him.
We ask Him to protect our plans.
To increase our income.
To restore our relationships.
To open doors.
To silence our enemies.
To make our ministries successful.
But when His Word confronts something we do not want to surrender…
Suddenly, we become very quiet.
We want His comfort.
But sometimes resist His correction.
We want His promises.
But hesitate before His commands.
We want Him to heal the consequences of our choices while remaining unwilling to turn from the choices themselves.
And still, Jesus calls.
Not because He enjoys exposing our hypocrisy.
But because He loves truth too much to leave us trusting a counterfeit.
In Matthew 7:23, Jesus describes those He rejects as people who “work iniquity.”
The Greek expression is:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν — hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian.
The word anomia refers to lawlessness or disregard for God's law.
The participle ergazomenoi describes those engaged in or practicing such conduct.
This is not a declaration that every believer who commits a sin is immediately condemned.
If that were the meaning, no human being could stand.
First John 1:8 plainly says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
But the very next verse gives hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
First John 1:9, KJV.
The distinction is not between people who have ever sinned and people who have never sinned.
All have sinned.
The distinction is between trusting Christ with a repentant heart and hiding behind religious claims while refusing His authority.
That is why this warning is not an invitation to obsess over whether you have achieved enough spiritual perfection.
It is an invitation to stop pretending.
To come into the light.
To stop treating repentance as something you will eventually get around to.
To stop confusing religious activity with spiritual life.
And to come to Jesus Himself.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heavy heart because you know there are things you have been hiding.
Maybe nobody knows about the addiction you keep returning to.
Maybe your marriage looks beautiful in photographs, but inside your home there are wounds you refuse to address.
Maybe you have learned how to encourage everyone else while privately growing cold toward God.
Maybe you have preached forgiveness while carrying resentment for years.
Maybe you have been living a double life, terrified that if people discovered the truth, everything you built would collapse.
Or maybe your struggle is different.
You genuinely love Jesus.
You hate the sin you keep fighting.
You repent, you pray, you stumble, you rise, and sometimes you wonder whether your repeated weakness means He has finally rejected you.
Please hear this carefully.
Matthew 7 is not telling a repentant, struggling believer that every failure proves Jesus never knew them.
Jesus also said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
John 6:37, KJV.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
These promises are not excuses to cling to sin.
They are reasons to run toward Christ instead of away from Him.
If you have fallen, come to Him.
If you are ashamed, come to Him.
If you have been pretending, stop pretending and come to Him.
If you have been trusting your religious achievements, lay them down and come to Him.
Do not wait until you can present yourself as someone worthy of mercy.
The whole reason we need mercy is that we cannot make ourselves worthy of it.
Remember Peter?
The man who declared his loyalty to Jesus with such confidence.
The man who insisted he was ready to die with Him.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denials.
Three times Peter denied knowing Jesus.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had walked on water toward Jesus could not even admit that he knew Him.
The man who had witnessed miracles collapsed under the pressure of a servant girl's question.
His courage failed.
His confidence shattered.
His own words accused him.
But that was not the end of Peter's story.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in John 21.
He did not pretend Peter's denial was harmless.
He addressed Peter personally, asking him about his love and entrusting him with responsibility to care for His sheep.
The fallen disciple was not beyond the reach of restoring grace.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this needs to remember tonight.
Your failure does not have to become your final identity.
But you cannot heal what you keep defending.
You cannot repent of what you insist on justifying.
You cannot surrender to Jesus while demanding that He leave every part of your life untouched.
Peter's story was not rewritten because betrayal suddenly became acceptable.
It was rewritten because the risen Christ is merciful, powerful, and able to restore those who turn to Him.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where our theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
The scandal is not merely that sinners have done terrible things.
The scandal is that human beings can become so religious that they forget how desperately they need a Savior.
The scandal is that we can build platforms in Jesus' name while quietly neglecting the character of Jesus.
The scandal is that we can become more concerned with being perceived as holy than with actually walking in holiness.
The scandal is that we can use spiritual language to conceal a heart unwilling to repent.
But grace?
Grace exposes the lie so that truth can set us free.
Grace confronts sin without declaring that the repentant sinner is beyond redemption.
Grace calls the proud to humility.
Grace calls the hypocrite to honesty.
Grace calls the wounded to the Healer.
Grace calls the rebellious to surrender.
And grace points every one of us to the cross, where Jesus Christ bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, just as the Scriptures testify in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
This is not a message about trying harder until God finally loves you.
This is the announcement that salvation is found in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
And when you truly receive His grace, you do not want to keep treating the sin that nailed Him to the cross as something harmless.
You begin to see sin differently.
Not merely as something that might ruin your reputation.
But as something that grieves the God who has shown you such astonishing mercy.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, your life begins to change.
Your apologies become more honest.
Your repentance becomes more than emotion.
Your forgiveness becomes more intentional.
Your prayers become less about impressing people and more about knowing God.
Your obedience becomes an expression of love rather than a desperate attempt to earn acceptance.
You may still have battles.
You may still need correction.
You may still need to confess the same weakness and seek help to overcome it.
But you are no longer content to build your home in the darkness.
You are learning to walk in the light.
And that brings us to the part of Jesus' warning that people often overlook.
Matthew 7:21–23 does not stand alone.
Immediately afterward, Jesus tells the parable of two builders.
One builds his house upon a rock.
The other builds upon sand.
Both houses face rain.
Both face floods.
Both are struck by winds.
From the outside, both may have looked secure before the storm.
But when the storm comes, only one remains standing.
Jesus explains that the wise builder is the person who hears His words and does them.
The foolish builder hears His words but does not put them into practice.
Matthew 7:24–27.
Do you understand what Jesus is showing us?
The issue is not merely what someone says about Him.
It is what foundation their life actually rests upon.
And the storm exposes what appearances once concealed.
Some people build their confidence on being raised in a Christian home.
Some build it on a baptismal certificate.
Some build it on the church they attend.
Some build it on the ministry they lead.
Some build it on the fact that they once prayed a prayer.
Some build it on spiritual experiences.
But none of those things, considered by themselves, can replace genuine faith in Jesus Christ.
Baptism matters.
Christian fellowship matters.
Ministry matters.
Prayer matters.
Obedience matters.
But they must never become substitutes for the Savior to whom they are meant to point.
Because when the storm comes, a religious reputation cannot hold you.
Only Christ can.
And perhaps this is why Jesus' words are so merciful even while they are terrifying.
He gives the warning before the final day.
While there is still time to repent.
While there is still time to abandon false confidence.
While there is still time to turn from darkness and come to the Light.
He does not leave us guessing about the danger.
He tells us plainly.
Not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” belongs to Him.
And that truth should make us humble, not arrogant.
It should never become a weapon for casually declaring that other people are unsaved.
You cannot see another person's heart as Jesus does.
You cannot pronounce His final judgment.
But you can examine your own life honestly before God.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 13:5:
This examination is not a command to abandon every assurance God has given His children.
It is a call to reject empty confidence and test what we profess.
Ask yourself:
Do I trust Jesus Christ as my Savior, or am I trusting the things I have done for Him?
When His Word confronts my sin, do I seek to repent, or do I continually search for ways to excuse myself?
Do I desire to know Him, even when nobody is watching?
Am I willing to receive correction?
Am I becoming more loving, truthful, humble, and obedient through His grace?
And when I fall, do I run to Him in repentance, or do I settle more deeply into hiding?
Do not answer these questions for the benefit of the people reading your comments.
Answer them before God.
Because this is not about performing another moment of public spirituality.
This is about truth.
And if you realize tonight that you have been living on religious autopilot, please do not turn this conviction into another promise that you will simply try harder tomorrow.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
Ask Him for a heart that loves what He loves.
Ask Him for the courage to turn away from what is destroying your soul.
Ask Him to make your faith genuine, your repentance sincere, and your obedience the fruit of His grace.
You do not need an impressive speech.
You need the Savior.
And if you are struggling to find words, you can pray something like this:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time worrying about how my faith looks to other people. You know the things I hide, the sins I excuse, the fears I carry, and the places where I have resisted Your truth. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely, to trust Your grace, and to follow You with a heart that truly belongs to You. I do not want a religious appearance without genuine faith. I want You. Change what needs to change in me. Lead me in Your truth. In Your name, Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula that guarantees salvation simply because the words have been spoken.
Our hope is Jesus Christ Himself, received through faith.
But sincere prayer can be an honest expression of a heart turning toward Him.
And if this message has exposed something in you, do not rush past it.
Sit with the Scriptures.
Open Matthew chapters 5 through 7.
Read the Sermon on the Mount in its full context.
Notice how Jesus confronts outward religion without inward righteousness.
Notice how He addresses anger, lust, retaliation, hypocrisy, prayer, money, anxiety, judgment, and the narrow way that leads to life.
Notice that His warning about “Lord, Lord” comes after He has already called His hearers to enter through the narrow gate and warned them about false prophets.
Jesus is not teaching a disconnected lesson about one frightening sentence.
He is calling people away from false righteousness and toward a life genuinely grounded in Him.
And if you want to understand the contrast even more deeply, read John 10:27–28:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.”
Notice the tenderness of those words.
“I know them.”
The same Savior who warns that some will hear “I never knew you” also speaks of His sheep as those He knows and to whom He gives eternal life.
Not temporary life earned through flawless performance.
Eternal life given by Him.
His sheep hear His voice and follow Him.
They belong to the Shepherd.
And the Shepherd holds them.
This is why the right response to Matthew 7 is neither careless presumption nor hopeless terror.
It is humble faith.
Repentance.
Surrender.
And confidence in the Savior who is faithful to His promises.
You do not need to spend your life trying to convince Jesus that your religious accomplishments make you worthy.
You need to know Him as the Savior who alone can make sinners right with God.
There is something else I want you to consider.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list, there may be a person who looks perfectly fine.
They post family pictures.
They celebrate birthdays.
They laugh in comment sections.
They share motivational quotes.
They may even post Bible verses.
But privately, they are exhausted.
They are drifting.
They have not prayed honestly in months.
They are wondering whether God still wants them.
Or perhaps they have become comfortable wearing Christianity as an identity while quietly ignoring Christ.
You do not know what God may use to reach them.
Maybe this article will not change everyone who reads it.
Maybe some will disagree.
Maybe others will feel convicted and decide to seek the Lord.
But if even one person is moved to open the Scriptures, repent sincerely, seek pastoral help, or return to serious discipleship, sharing the truth will have been worthwhile.
Not to make yourself appear spiritual.
Not to prove that you are better than anyone.
But because the Gospel is too important to keep hidden out of embarrassment.
Not to publicly shame them.
But to invite them into a conversation that could matter deeply.
And please, do not leave without being honest about what this passage has stirred in your own heart.
Or share a testimony of how Jesus has been teaching you the difference between outward religion and a living relationship with Him.
You do not have to reveal private sins or painful details publicly.
God hears the prayers you cannot put into a comment.
But sometimes one honest testimony gives another struggling person the courage to stop pretending.
And sometimes a simple request for prayer reminds someone that they do not have to fight alone.
Not because these words are more important than Scripture, but because you may want to return to Matthew 7 when your heart needs to remember what Jesus actually said.
Read it again when pride begins creeping in.
Read it again when religious activity starts replacing private devotion.
Read it again when shame tempts you to believe that repentance is pointless.
Let the warning humble you.
Let the Gospel restore your hope.
And let the Word of God have the final authority.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish another Christian post that disappears into a crowded newsfeed.
But to help people keep returning to Scripture, to the truth about Jesus Christ, and to the daily work of growing as His disciples.
If you have been following these messages and they have helped you pray, repent, understand the Bible, or find encouragement in Christ, I want to invite you to go deeper.

Our prayer is that this community will be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, wounded people are not treated as disposable, and the grace of Jesus Christ is proclaimed without turning it into permission to remain in sin.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond inspirational moments into serious engagement with God's Word.
Because one emotional article cannot replace a life of discipleship.
You need Scripture.
You need prayer.
You need fellowship with faithful believers.
You need a local church where biblical teaching, worship, accountability, and mutual care are practiced.
And you need the daily grace of God as you learn to follow Jesus.
But please understand something important.
It does not purchase forgiveness.
It does not make you more saved.
It does not prove that your faith is genuine.
And it should never replace your responsibility to care for your family, honor existing financial commitments, or support your local church as you believe Scripture directs.
The Bible teaches generous, willing giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
The Gospel is not for sale.
Your worth before God is not measured by your financial contribution.
You can still help by praying, reading, sharing the articles, inviting others, and using the free discipleship resources.
We would be grateful to have you walk with us in this mission.
Not as customers purchasing a spiritual blessing.
But as fellow travelers who believe the truth of Jesus Christ is worth proclaiming, teaching, and sharing.
Because the world does not need more polished religious appearances.
It needs the true Gospel.
It needs people who will speak about repentance without forgetting grace.
People who will proclaim forgiveness without minimizing sin.
People who will defend biblical truth without abandoning compassion.
People who will remind the broken that Jesus still receives those who come to Him.
And people who understand that the purpose of ministry is not to make a human name famous.
It is to glorify the name of Jesus Christ.
But before you leave this article, I want to return to the scene where we began.
The final day.
The crowd is gone.
The titles are gone.
The applause is gone.
Everything that once made you feel important has fallen silent.
And you stand before Jesus.
What will matter then?
Not whether your name was recognized in Christian circles.
Not whether your posts received thousands of reactions.
Not whether you had a ministry people admired.
Not whether you appeared more righteous than the person sitting beside you in church.
What will matter is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether your hope rests in His grace.
Whether the faith you profess is real.
And whether the life you lived bore the fruit of that faith.
There is no need to manufacture an impressive religious résumé for the One who already knows the heart.
Come to Him now.
While the invitation of the Gospel is being proclaimed.
While you can still hear His words.
While you can still turn away from the false foundations that cannot save you.
If you have been hiding behind religion, come out of hiding.
If you have been trusting your own goodness, put your trust in Christ.
If you have been using grace as an excuse to cherish sin, repent.
If you have been crushed by guilt despite sincerely turning to Jesus, remember His promises.
If you have wandered, return to the Shepherd.
If you have fallen, seek His restoring mercy.
And if you have never truly trusted Him, do not settle for simply knowing the right words to say.
Believe the Gospel.
Turn to the living Savior.
Follow Him.
Because the most important question is not whether people believe you are a Christian.
It is whether you truly belong to Christ.
And when everything else is stripped away, the only foundation that will stand is the One Jesus Himself told us to build upon.

The tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life with nothing to show the world—but reaching eternity with a lifetime of religious achievements and discovering that you had never truly come to Jesus.
